name: Zinc pyrithione
lead: Zinc pyrithione (pyrithione zinc, ZPT) is a zinc coordination complex with antifungal and antibacterial properties. It is the active ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos and body washes and is used for seborrheic dermatitis; it is also used in antifouling paints and some textiles.[1][2]

For appearance, its role is on the scalp: by acting against the Malassezia yeasts associated with flaking and itch, it clears visible dandruff flakes and calms scalp redness, so hair and shoulders look cleaner and the scalp looks healthier. Reviews describe zinc pyrithione products as market leaders among topical treatments for seborrheic dermatitis.[6] The same compound appears in treatment of pityriasis versicolor, a Malassezia-related condition that causes patchy lighter or darker skin on the upper trunk, neck and arms.[2][8]

It has been used in dandruff products for decades and is approved as an over-the-counter dandruff ingredient in the US.[3] Its regulatory status differs by region: Wikipedia reports that the EU has barred its use in cosmetics since December 2021, citing a reproductive-toxicity classification and environmental concerns.[2]
infobox: OTC dandruff active (US); barred in EU cosmetics since 2021[2]

paras: The main use is relief of dandruff symptoms; a US over-the-counter label states it is for relief of dandruff symptoms and warns against use on wounds or damaged skin or on children under 12 unless directed by a physician.[3] It is also used in paints, coatings and odor-control textiles; Wikipedia notes use in antibacterial household sponges and textile treatments.[2]

Seborrheic dermatitis produces skin flaking, redness and itching, and its pathobiology involves Malassezia yeast, inflammation, sebum production and barrier disruption. A 2023 review of topical therapeutics reports that zinc pyrithione products are the market leaders among the available treatments.[6]

Narrative reviews list zinc pyrithione among first-line topical options for pityriasis (tinea) versicolor alongside ketoconazole, selenium sulphide and terbinafine, noting that most patients respond to topical antifungals and that relapse is common because Malassezia is part of normal skin flora.[7][8][9] Reviews also state oral terbinafine is not effective for this condition.[8]

Proposed antifungal mechanisms include disrupting membrane transport and, according to a 2011 yeast study, raising intracellular copper to damage iron-sulfur proteins.[2] Zinc compounds more broadly have a long history in dermatology.[4]

A 2023 pharmaceutics review of topical delivery notes that Malassezia on the skin surface is effectively targeted, while yeast deeper in the follicle may receive less zinc pyrithione, which the authors suggest as a basis for re-colonisation after treatment. The same review reports that amounts entering systemic circulation from topical use are well below toxic thresholds, while elevated zinc in the living epidermis warrants further investigation.[6] The compound has low water solubility (about 8 ppm at neutral pH), which is why it is retained on skin as a suspension in shampoos and also suits outdoor paints.[2]

Wikipedia reports that the EU classifies it as a Category 1B reproductive toxicant, that laboratory studies have linked it to DNA damage in skin cells, and that US rules allow up to 2% in rinse-off and 0.25% in leave-on products.[2] A separate review literature documents its toxicity to marine organisms as an antifouling biocide.[5] Wikipedia also cites Swedish and Danish studies indicating it degrades in wastewater treatment and biodegrades quickly, though continuous leaching from boat paint may be toxic to aquatic life.[2]

Zinc pyrithione shampoos have served as the comparator in several dandruff trials, including those against piroctone olamine and ketoconazole shampoos; Wikipedia cites a 1985 study of a zinc pyrithione shampoo and a 2002 trial against ketoconazole in severe dandruff.[2] A 2013 randomized clinical trial compared shampoos based on potentiated zinc pyrithione and on zinc pyrithione with climbazole for therapeutic efficacy against dandruff.[10] A randomized trial published in 2011 used scalp stratum corneum sampling to relate histamine levels to itch resolution during treatment of dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis.[11]

An open trial from 1980 examined a zinc pyrithione shampoo in tinea versicolor.[12] A 2018 multicenter randomized trial examined how the scalp environment influences hair cuticle integrity as hair emerges.[13] A review of zinc therapy in dermatology covers zinc pyrithione among topical uses.[4] Antiviral activity has been reported only in cell culture, with no human clinical evidence noted.[2] Laboratory work has also examined zinc pyrithione as an inhibitor of proteasomal deubiquitinases in cancer-research settings.[15]

Zinc pyrithione is sold under many shampoo brands and as the raw material Zinc Omadine; US rules allow up to 2% in rinse-off and 0.25% in leave-on products.[2] The EU classification as a Category 1B reproductive toxicant led to a cosmetic ban from December 2021, so formulations sold in the EU differ from those in the US.[2] In antifouling paints it is one of several booster biocides that replaced organotin compounds after restrictions on tributyltin in 1987, and reviews document its effects on marine species.[14][5]

timeline.event: EU bars its use in cosmetics.[2]

card.summary: The classic dandruff-shampoo antifungal; long used OTC in the US but barred from EU cosmetics since 2021.
card.note: Evidence is for dandruff; regulatory status differs between US and EU.

quick.overview:
Zinc pyrithione is the active in many dandruff shampoos. It acts against the yeasts linked to flaking and scalp itch.

It is a standard comparator in dandruff trials. It is not a hair-growth treatment.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to disrupt fungal membrane transport and raise intracellular copper, damaging iron-sulfur proteins.
quick.risks: US labels warn against use on damaged skin or in young children. The EU classifies it as a reproductive toxicant and has barred it in cosmetics since 2021; it is also toxic to aquatic life as an antifouling agent.

chain: Antifungal action against scalp Malassezia yeast
Fewer visible flakes and less itch and scaling
angle.text: Shampoos and body washes containing zinc pyrithione are used to clear dandruff flakes and scaling on the scalp, which changes how hair and the scalp look day to day. Users apply it as a medicated wash rather than a hair-growth product.
